make a highly selective reading of the Qur'an implies that an attempt in good faith to develop an
anthology of the highlights and for a good cause of motivating the Muslim youth to draw closer to the
Divine Message should not be met with resistance, remaining mindful that 'Allah alone guides
whoever He wills as it is only He who knows best the ones who are amenable to guidance’ — 29:56.

Thus giving my soul some comfort, I found guidance in one of the key expressions in 03:07, viz. Umm
ul-Kitab, i.e. Mother of the Book or Essence of the Qur'an. Hence, for purposes of this exercise and
remaining in spiritual and physical purity, the essence of each Sirah was captured followed by
identification of the common and variant themes between and among the one hundred and fourteen
Sirahs.

The language and narrative of the Qur'an is deliberately left with gaps so that the reader may actively
participate in its comprehension, thereby stimulating thinking process. The Qur'an is not for a passive
reader; it is for conscious people. Furthermore, the Qur'anic Ayat/Statements appear to be repeated
several times. The purpose is to lay stress on certain teachings.

Nonetheless, there are ensembles of narratives which are presented with a specific purpose, but none of
these usually present a complete picture in one place. A piece told ina given Sirah is likely to be Sirah-
specific. For example, the narrative about Abraham" appears in Sirah six, twenty-one, fifty-one, sixty
and twenty other instances. In each of these, a different part of his biography is told. Stirah Six is mainly
addressed to the idolaters and criticism of idolatry figures prominently in it. Thus, the Sirah selects
from Abraham's” life that incident in which he is shown as refuting his idolatrous people.

The connection between the incident and the Siirah's theme is obvious, both making the point that the
then idolaters of Pagan Makkah, if they wished to follow Abraham” as their spiritual ancestor, they
must abandon idolatry and worship the One True Allah, a point relevant for all times for those
practicing idolatry and worshiping saints and spirits, objects and entities, real or myth, besides One
God, Allah.

Similarly, while Moses" is treated in great detail and at length, the episode highlighting his role as a
liberator, a lawgiver and a channel of Divine Revelation - that resembles the most with profile of
Muhammad's Mission - has been retained and so is the narrative of Jesus.”

The narrative about the creation of Adam and the fall of Satan and Adam, and the episodes from the
chronicles of history and other thematic issues are recounted on several occasions. But consideration
has been given to the choice of the one at 07: 11-27 that appears to give a compact account of the episode
captured in Divine-Adam-Satan dialogue and the subsequent events. Thus, the exercise endeavors to
limit itself to one Ayah/Statement or narrative in each case, and cross referenced to facilitate better
understanding of the subject, its context as well as provide the whole message.

There are some eight hundred and eighty three Ayat/Statements that were revealed in response to
specific situations and circumstances, and/or in connection with a particular person or a group. For
example, 49:11 contains three injunctions relating to social behavior:

o No one should ever jeer or mock the other, for it is quite possible that they may be better than them.
o Their women should not ever jeer or mock other women, who may after all be better than them.
o Do not find faults with one another, and do not taunt by using offensive nicknames for one another.

The first came for one Thabit Ibn Kais Ibn Shammas who mocked someone for his low social status in
the presence of the Prophet”. The second was a stern warning to Sayedah A’isha (613-678) and
Sayedah Hafsa who made sarcastic remarks about Sayedah Umm Salamah - all three were wives of the
Prophet”. The third was revealed in response to two complaints - one by Sayedah Hafsa, wife of the
Prophet’, and the other by one Ibn al Dahak.

Notwithstanding their specificity to individuals and time, all three injunctions are for general
application and for all times. This compilation covers most of these injunctions. The Ayat/Statements
sketching out the scenes of the Time of Resurrection and Judgment, and the Afterlife have also been
selectively retained as some of the seven hundred and fifty Statements dealing with natural phenomena.

title: Allah Speaks to you, us and them individually and collectively through His ennobled Prophet
ocr_text:
Allah Speaks to you, us and them individually and collectively through His ennobled Prophet
Muhammad, Allah bless him always with honor. His Speech is filled with providential care and
guidance. There are over five hundred Ayat/Statements where the Divine Voice speaks through a set of
imperatives signifying an emphasis on matter of faith; like Oud - say, tell, declare, pronounce, proclaim;
O The Prophet/Messenger; O Prophet's Wives; O The Faithful; O Descendants of Adam; O Followers of
Former Divine Scriptures; O Israelites; O The Disbelievers; O People of the World. More important and
non-repetitive of these imperatives have been taken as the highlights.

There are certain passages which talk about the ultimate reality of all things, of the real and final nature
of the universe, of mind and the interrelation of mind and matter. A fair sample of such passages and
almost all Ayat/Statements speaking of righteous behavior and of practical life have been retained.

Overall and in resonance with split of the Qur'anic subjects, sampling of beliefs occupy the larger part;
morals and social behavior come next, followed by legal provisions. This constitutes one hundred and
ten five Ayat/Statements, or approximately fourteen percent of the full Qur'anic text, thereby making the
volumetric size considerably concise, yet presenting a fairly representative sample of the essence of the
Qur'an and its profound excellence.

The Qur'an is a unique and unmatched masterpiece of Arabic literature. The spirit, the beauty, the
eloquence, the depth and the comprehensiveness of the Arabic text can never be captured by any other
language. Translations can be dull and convey the apparent meaning, but remain devoid of the true spirit,
divine sanctity and powerful beauty of its eloquence and hence its impact. Strongly mindful of these
limitations and my inadequacies, I seek Allah's guidance and support to accomplish a faithful translation
embedded with true spirit.

This work is not strictly a translation. It is a blend of translation and brief explication, wherever
necessary, by adding words to make the translation comprehensible, dubbed as ‘paraphrasing’. It
purposely avoids long wording in parentheses, and does not burden the text with footnotes. Extreme care
has been taken to capture the closest meaning in English of every word/expression in Arabic of an
Ayah/Statement, and not to let it smudge with extended language. The closest meanings are expressed in
straight type script appearing in bold; the extended meanings appear in italic script. The two embedded
in each other present one simple, harmonious and expressive Ayah/Statement in modern and friendly
English. Best endeavors been have exercised to convey the Truth as the Whole Truth.

It is quite probable that an Ayah/Statement may not be understood on its first reading but clarity should
develop on the second or later readings. Similarly, a set of words or phrases may offer more than one
interpretation; hence there could be considerable variance among available translations as well as
whether or not the translator is a Muslim. In order to understand certain Ayat/Statements one might also
need to get proper perspective, notwithstanding that understanding would be influenced by one's
attitude, prejudice, and interest in Islam and The Qur'an.

This book is not and can never be a substitute for The Qur'an. It is only intended to motivate men and
women, young and old, to draw closer to The Qur'an by reading and understanding the highlights of
Allah's Final Message to humanity conveyed through His Final Prophet Muhammad, Allah bless him
always with honor.

The Qur'an is not paper and ink. It is a Guide for ethics, morality, decency, righteousness and societal
change with focus on shaping one’s life on Allah's Will. It is blessed and full of blessings. Let blessings
of The Qur'an live in us, and enliven our souls!

Badr Hashemi

Grand Rapids, Mich.

The Recipient of the Qur'an
Muhammad

The Seal of the Prophets and Mercy for Humanity
(Allah bless him always with honor)

Muhammad was born in Makkah, a commercial metropolis and a pilgrims’ hub in the Arabian
Peninsula, in 570. He was the only child of his parents — Sayed Abd Allah bin Abd Al-Muttalib Al-
Hashemi and Sayedah Aminah bint Wahb Al-Zuhriyya. Shepherd in early life, and then, as a young
person, he was a successful merchant. He married Sayedah Khadijah in 595 at the age of twenty-
five. They made a happy couple and became the parents of two sons and four daughters.

Muhammad was popularly reputed as friendly, trustworthy and a gentleman of impeccable
character. As he was attaining maturity, he was getting deeply disturbed by social and moral
environment around him. He found the idolatry and fetishism vulgar and social injustices
distressing. He increasingly began to search for a response to his own agony at the injustice and
chaos around him by resorting to meditation. He would go away from home for several days ina
row and stay ina small cave on Mountal-Nur, named Hira’, on the outskirts of Makkah.

The seclusion continued for a considerable period of time. It was in 610 that he underwent an
experience of his life in Hira’. It was one night, after midnight, during the last ten days of the month
of Ramadan, that he received the Divine Call. It was the beginning of the Divine Prophetic Mission
for Muhammad, Allah bless him always. The Mission focused on three principal themes. First,
Allah - the Lord Unitary, is the absolute source of all social, religious and legal authority. Second,
all human beings are equal regardless of lineage, race and color. Third, the governance must be
based on humaneness and social responsibility.

Prophet Muhammad's life and mission made an overwhelming appeal to the masses. It uplifted the
status of women, gave rights to the under privileged, and regulated the moral and social life of the
disenfranchised. Obviously, it undermined the social and political authority of the ruling and the
privileged in Makkah. They felt threatened. They started a systemic campaign of intimidation and
persecution of the newly formed nucleus of Prophet Muhammad's followers. The campaign of
oppression and torture continued for ten long years.

Finally, Allah” guided His Last Prophet Muhammad" and his companions to emigrate to
Madinah in 622. It took him several years to strive and battle against tyranny, oppression and social
injustice. He created a generation of highly inspired Faithful for whom his words were the guiding
star of their lives. His words continue to be the guiding star for millions - past, present and future.
The Qur'an portrays this group of the Faithful in Statement 110, Surah 03 * Al ‘Imran. It says:

- You are the noblest community that has ever been raised up for the human race.

- As you enjoin wholesome justice, equity and fairness, and, you forbid all that is
wrong.

- As you firmly believe in the oneness, supremacy and un-shared divinity of Allah.

It was in Madinah that he, slowly but steadily, set up the foundations of the first Islamic Welfare
State. He wrote the charter that guaranteed the political and economic rights of all men and
women. He established the code of ethics for times of peace and times of war. He set a track record
of personal examples of social responsibility and egalitarianism. It is to this time that the Muslim
Faithful, around the world, are inspired to re-establish this model state as a political and economic
system.

While he was approaching the sixty-third year of his life, the Last Prophet" prepared himself and
his family for the Hajj - the only Hajj that he performed in his lifetime. On this occasion he was
pleased to be in the company of over hundred thousand Believing Faithful who gathered at Arafat

ocr_text:
on Friday, the 09" of Dul-Hijjah, in 632. He addressed the Faithful from Mount al-Rahmah. The
essence of his address sets the foundation of his teachings and Mission for all times:

- Treat the life and property of every Muslim as a sacred trust.

- Hurt no one so that no one may hurt you.

- Do not inflict inequity and, as a consequence, do not cause
yourselves to suffer inequity.

- You are forbidden for all times to get involved in usury business.

- Treat your spouse with kindness. They are your partners in life
and faithful helpers.

- Stay fully committed to the worshipful obedience of One
Allah....Offer the daily Mandatory Prayers....Fast during the
whole month of Ramadan......Give a part of your wealth in
Zakat.

- All human beings are equal. The superiority of one over the
other is only by ones reverence to Allah, deeds of righteousness
and responsible social behavior.

- The Muslim Community constitutes One Family.

This appeared to be his last public address. This was also the time when he received the last
revelation (05:03), which wrapped-up his Divine Prophetic Mission to humanity. The Qur'an was
completed.

Back in Madinah from the Hajj, he was frail, weak and unwell. He was running intense fever. In the
forenoon of hot sandy summer of 632, while he was in his chamber, he was preparing to leave this
world, he raised his index finger and eyes to the Heaven and called out: "Better the next world...'
With these words he peacefully left this world for a better world. His body was respectfully laid to
rest in the place where he breathed his last.

The green dome of the Masjid al-Nabi al-Sharif in Madinah al-Munawarah makes the canopy of
his resting place.

May Allah, His angels and all righteous souls send their wholesome blessings on Muhammad.
Muhammad, the person - Gem ofa Person. Muhammad, the Prophet - Gem ofa Prophet.

Glossary

Allah — It is an Arabic expression, a proper name for the Almighty and Supreme Being: The One God,
singular, who does not have a gender, parents, siblings, spouse, daughters and/or sons. Allah is above
and beyond all description; there is nothing whatever like Him. Faith in One Allah is the fulcrum of
Islamic monotheism and obedience to His Will is the focus of the Muslim way of life. Allah is not a
contraction of al-ilah, but a totally different word. While pronouncing the word Allah, the stress in
accent is on letter 'L' like 'b' in abbey. It appears 2,697 times in The Qur'an. Names and Attributes of
Allah, al-Asma al-Husna, are traditionally enumerated as ninety-nine epithets, on which is based its
systematic expositions about the divine essence —dhat - and its attributes — sifat.

Ayah/Ayat (pl) — Sign, parable, symbol, miraculous event, a Statement of The Qur'an. I have retained
the Arabic expression without translation because it cannot be rendered appropriately in English.
Translators usually translate Ayah as 'Verse' which I consider absolutely incorrect because The Qur'an
is not poetry to have a verse or a set of verses.

Blasphemy - Speech or writing that is derogatory to Allah*” which is the closest translation of Sacred
Text expression of takdhib - 'giving a lie, denial’ and iftira, ‘fabrication’, In as muchas Allah*”” and His
Messages represent the ultimate truth, blasphemy is denial of that truth or propagation ofa falsehood in
its place. Blasphemy by denial (takdhib) is the outright rejection of revealed religious truths, such as
the revelations and warnings of Allah's Emissaries, revelation and inspiration, warning, and the
announcements of the Time of Resurrection and Judgment, and finally the Meeting with Allah*"” (Q.
06:31; 10:45; 23:33; 25:11; 82:09)
Blessing - Allah°“” bestows blessings on humankind by way of creation and ordering of life and the
universe, sustenance, progeny, material wealth, health, protection, deliverance from enemies, and so
on. Expression of gratitude for Allah°”'s blessings is a fundamental obligation and failure to do so is
tantamount to disbelief. (Q. 14:28; 16:114.)
Dhikr — Translated as remembrance, commemoration, admonition, etc. In its context, it implies
following the Qur'an and keeping of the oracles of Allah; Remembrance of Allah. The expression and
its various forms occur 292 times in the Qur'an.
Hadith/Ahadith (pl) — A corpus of explicit statement, text, maxim, saying or action attributed to the
Prophet Muhammad"”; always naming both the transmitter(s) and the original source. Sometimes
translated as the Tradition. A number of compilations made after about two centuries of the demise of
the Prophet"” are regarded as authentic on the subject; these comprise: Al-Bokhari, Al-Muslim, Al-
Tirmidi, Sunan Ibn Majah, Sunan Abu Dawood, Sunan Nesa'i, Mauta Imam Malik, and K@fi, etc. See
also 'Sunnah' below, where the two are comingled.

Haram - Sacred, forbidden; Sanctuary surrounding the Ka'bah (Makkah); also the Prophet's Masjid in
the premises of his final resting place in Madinah.

Hajj —The annual pilgrimage to Makkah in the month of Dhul-Hijjah, the twelfth month of the Islamic
Calendar; required of all adult Muslims once in their lifetime, if possible. The Hajj stations comprise of
al-Masjid al-Haram, Mina, 'Arafat (essential parts of the Hajj ceremonies occur here) and Muzdalifah
(a location some half-way between Mina and ‘Arafat where the pilgrims returning from ‘Arafat spend
the night in worshipful devotion) - all in Makkah and within its 13-mile periphery. It is one of the five
Pillars of the Faith of Islam.

Halal- A practice, custom or an act sanctified/made lawful by a Divine Decree contained in The Qur'an.
Itis the opposite of Haram.

Sama'/Samawat' (pl) is normally translated as 'the heavens’; in fact, the expression is a metonym for
all the stars, moon, sun, galaxies, nebulae, etc. Thus, it has been paraphrased as 'the cosmos.’ The other
connotation is the spiritual plane of eternal happiness. In Arabic Sacred Text, however, there have
always been two separate expressions used, sama’ and jannah. The word sama’ is used for the cosmos
and the word jannah denotes Paradise, the land of eternal bliss, the permanent home of the righteous
believers, and the opposite of Hell. 'As-Sama' has also been used in The Qur'an to imply the realm of
unperceivable to which ascend the good words and good deeds.

Hijrah — The emigration of Prophet Mohammad"” from Makkah to Madinah; the year it occurred 622
is the base-year of commencement of the Muslim era/calendar. The Hijrah Calendar is different from
the Arabic Calendar.

About BH

Badr Hashemi (BH) was born (1944) and raised in a religious family
environment which inherited a legacy of the centuries' old tradition of
dispensing values, virtues and education. He completed the elementary
learning and partly memorized The Qur'an while under ten and continued
with learning the Arabic language, grammar and exegesis of The Qur'an and
Hadith in parallel with formal western education in social sciences and
development studies.

BH attended sandwich courses at Al-Azhar in The Qur'anic Arabic and
lectures in interpretation of The Qur'an and Fiqh by Shykh Ali Al-Tantawi
(Faqih) in Cairo, and Shykh Yusuf Al-Qaradawi (Faqih) in Qatar. He had
periodic learning sessions with Professor A. J. Arberry (Roman Catholic,
translator of The Qur'an and Ahadith, etc.) during the mid-sixties while BH
was a student at the University of Cambridge (UK), and, later in the late-
eighties with Muhammad Asad (Jewish convert to Islam, translator of The
Qur'an and Ahadith, etc.) in Gibraltar.

BH is a Professional Economist and a Fellow of the World Bank Institute of
Development Economics in Washington DC, and the United Nations Asian
Development Institute. Worked as a civil servant in Pakistan and was part of
the international civil service with the United Nations. He has been a keynote
speaker at international seminars/conferences in Europe, the Middle East-
North Africa, and the Far East; widely traveled with long periods of stay in
the Arab Middle East and North A frica.

Well versed in Arabic and English and well read in the Torah, the Psalms, the
Injil, Islamic history and culture, ancient civilizations and comparative
religions, BH has held interactive discussions with Jewish Rabbis and
Christian Priests in North America and Western Europe. He has visited
various sites and places of history enumerated in the Torah, the Injil and The
Qur'an — scattered from the Nile Delta through the Levant to Babylon.

BH initiated work on'English Translation and Paraphrasing of The Qur'an' in
1999 with the aim of understanding The Qur'an with The Qur'an. This
research project has progressed to reach its conclusion. Five of its six
volumes are available from The Holy Qur'an’ Research Foundation, 60-C,
Nazimuddin Road, F-8/4, Islamabad. In addition, he has published ‘The
Divine 99’ available from Islamic Research Institute, International Islamic
University, Faisal Campus, Islamabad, Pakistan.

He is also exploring the principal thematic issues in the Hadith literature that
form the common heritage between the Shiite and the Sunni schools of
thought in Islam. BH can be reached via email at hashemibadr@gmail.com
and visited at www.quranhighlights.com

title: Islam — Surrender/submission to the Will of Allah; theoretically the term is applied to the religion
ocr_text:
Islam — Surrender/submission to the Will of Allah; theoretically the term is applied to the religion
proclaimed by all Prophets of Allah from Noah to Mohammad, Allah bless them all. However, the
name has eventually become synonymous with the followers of The Qur'an and Prophet Mohammad”.
Jihad — Struggle, effort, endeavor, a state of striving for the Cause of Allah — utilizing all physical,
mental and spiritual faculties in accordance with the Shari'ah/Muslim Law to suppress tyranny, ensure
the right of an individual to home and freedom, prevent persecution in religion and guarantee freedom
of belief to all people; it also includes war/qital - there are different opinions as to the circumstances
under which it becomes necessary. Jehad is a non-violent activity and is not meant to impose Islam or
spread it by force — Q. 02:190, 256; 03:20, 104; 04:90; 05:14; 10:100; 16:125; 24:54; 109:01-06. The
expression is also applied to a person's own struggle against one's baser impulses. The expression
occurs about 41 times in its various forms.

Jinn — Affirmed by the Qur'an as Allah's creation, are the conscious beings, intelligent, corporal that
cannot be seen by human beings. The Qur'an presents the Jinn, like humans, as good or bad. The
expression occurs about 201 times in its different forms.

Ka'bah - The cube-like structure within the al-Masjid al-Haram in Makkah, which is clad with black
covering. It is towards this site that the Muslims direct their Prayers; but do not worship it.

Madinah - ~250 miles north of Makkah, the name given to the agricultural settlement of Yathrib after
emigration of the Prophet”.

Masjid - Usually translated as Mosque; place of worship for Muslims where the Salat/Salah is
performed - daily five times in congregation.

Makkah - the Epicenter of Islam and houses the Holy Ka'bah; birthplace of Prophet Mohammad". It
lies about 45 miles east of the Red Sea port of Jeddah, Arabian Peninsula.

Muslim - Derived from Islam, means surrender/submission of one's being to One Allah and obedience
to Divine Revelations. In contemporary context, it implies obedience to The Qur'an and Prophet
Mohammad”; the one who has accepted the Faith of Islam.

Prophet/Emissary - Two terms used for prophethood, expressed as nabiyy and rasil in the Arabic
Sacred Text; the later denotes a divine office which does not necessarily bring a new Shari'ayah/Divine
Law; the former entails bringing a new/revised Divine Law. Prophet Mohammad" is called by both.
Rasiil is also used for angle-envoys sent to Abraham"” and Lot”.

P—appearing as mounted” on the name of a Prophet of Allah implies 'Peace be upon him.’

Satan — Shaytan in Arabic occurs about 88 times in The Qur'an. Arabic/Qur'anic dictionaries term it as
the one remote from all that is good and true; exceedingly evil; rebellious; obstinate; perverse; far from
Allah's mercy; the impulses in human soul which run counter to truth and morality. It does not
necessarily mean devil.
The Qur'an —Also transliterated Qur'an, Koran, Qur'an, Coran, Kuran, Quraan, Kura'n and Al-Qur'an.
Divine Scripture revealed by Allah to Prophet Mohammad”. It is the absolute and unchanging Word of
Allah with spiritually nourishing latent content: a divine, eternal and dynamic text. Among other
matters, The Qur'an identifies scientific phenomena including creation of cosmos, space and earth,
astronomy, earth science, water cycle, animal and plant kingdoms, human reproduction, etc. The term
qur'an which, whenever it appears without the definite article 'al’, i.e. Al-Qur'an (The Qur'an), denotes a
solemn recitation, recital or discourse. In all its manifestations, it appears about 89 times in The Qur'an;
it comprises 30 Chapters of equal length, and consists of 114 Stirahs of unequal length. See 'Siirah’
below.
Rabb - The expression is used for Allah about 969 times in The Qur'an. It is usually rendered in English
as Lord, which I consider as too limited to convey essence of the expression 'Rabb.' Hence, I have
retained it as it appears in the Arabic Scared Text. It conveys not only the idea of fostering, bringing up
and nourishing but also that of regulating, completing, accomplishing, sustaining and perfection. It
also means originator of things and their combiner to create new forms. The lexicons of Arabic
language speak of all of them, and more, when they give the detailed meaning of the root Rabb, the
stress in accent is on letter 'b' as 'b' in abbey.

Ramadan — Fasting from dawn-break till sunset/dusk; abstinence from foods, drinks, smoking, wife-
husband cohabitation, and human baser desires during 29 or 30 days of Ramadan — ninth month of the
Islamic Calendar. Obligatory on all adult Muslims, except for reasons of old age, sickness and travel,
etc. Itis one of the five Pillars of the Faith of Islam.

Salat/Salah —A series of acts/postures of worship, encompassing spirit, mind and body, performed ina
fully described manner by Muslims five times a day — early morning, afternoon, late afternoon, dusk

title: and night, preferably in groups, facing toward the Ka'bah; including the special group prayer of midday
ocr_text:
and night, preferably in groups, facing toward the Ka'bah; including the special group prayer of midday

on Friday. It comprises short recitations from The Qur'an. It is the cardinal form of worship for the

Muslims and is one of the five Pillars of the Faith of Islam.

Sunnah - The body of recorded words, actions, gestures and practices of Prophet Mohammad” that

have been established as legally binding. This material constitutes the second foundation of the Faith of

Islam and its legal system, The Qur'an being the first and prime source. See also ‘Hadith' above, where

the two are comingled.

Sirah/Suwar (pl) — Literally means a fence, enclosure, or any part of a structure. In the Qur'anic

context it means an embodiment of a collection of Ayat, which may vary in length from 286 to 3 Ayat.

The Qur'an comprises 114 Sirah.

‘Umrah — Mini Hajj; consists three worshipful acts of al-ihram, al-tawaf and al-sa'y - all are performed

within the premises of al-Masjid al-Haram in Makkah.

SWT - This is the Acronym for Arabic 'Subhanahu wa Ta'ala' meaning Allah is pure of having partners,

and He is exalted from having a child.

Zakah/Zakat — The word is linked to zaka (to be pure); it implies expiation or purification of one's

material possessions, i.e. money, wealth and property - a fixed proportion of which is supposed to be

paid out yearly by the well-to-do Muslims as obligatory charity to the poor and/or for other defined
causes. It provides social security and is an important parameter of Islamic fiscal system. It is also one
of the five Pillars of the Faith of Islam.

translated as the sense required, but not left untranslated as it constitutes a party of the Divine
Revelation.

Transliteration Guide

There are ten characters in Arabic alphabet w:

e same sounds are some times spelt in more than

one way, and the same letter may be used to represent more than one sound , e.g. ‘C’ represent ‘S’
in ‘face’ but ‘K’ in ‘cloth’. Arabic spellings are much more regular and one letter or symbol
represents just one sound.

Over the years several attempts have been made to bridge the gap for transliterating the Arabic
sound correctly into the English language. Currently, a combination of three different techniques
are employed for transliteration of certain Arabic alphabets, which do not have an equivalent in
the English language.

1. Placing a macron (-) over the English alphabets to indicate long vowels of the
Arabic language; for example:
Iman 04) Rasal Js) Inj = de!
2. Placements of dots (.) under certain English alphabets; for example:
Hajj & Muhammad sins Tawaf Gijb Salat suc
3. Underlining (_) certain alphabet or combination of alphabets; for example:
Uthman ola Hadith ews
Notwithstanding the foregoing, there remains a considerable confusion in the systems in practice.
A normally authoritative and careful encyclopedia employs, within the space of a dozen pages,
three different versions of a common name like ‘Quraish’. At least three more spellings of the
word are commonly used, and another twelve spellings are theoretically justifiable according to
the various principles of transliteration of Arabic.

Thus, in practice building a usable romanization involves tradeoffs between Arabic and English
characters. Pure transcriptions are generally not possible as Arabic contains sounds and
distinctions alien to English. The choice of transliteration for this Study has been made as

Journeying Through The Qur'an

@ The Qur'an is meant for the welfare of humanity. Thus, it shall forever be guarded against all corruption and
all attempts to destroy it.

@ Mockery and opposition to the Word of Allah would never go unpunished. Whenever it is read with faith and
reverence, it serves as a healing of hearts and spiritual ailments and a blessing.

@ The main theme is the Faith, and the main issues that surround it: Allah's Unity and Supremacy, submission to
Him, His Revelations, the Resurrection and its correlatives. This life is transient to another permanent life after
the Resurrection, where everyone will be rewarded in accordance with ones performance in this life. The losers
will be those who deny Allah's Sovereignty and neglect His Guidance.

@ Everyone's dignity must be respected, regardless of one's religion, race, ethnicity, gender, or social status. It is
by Divine Will that human creation follows different religions.

@ There is neither any coercion in matters of faith nor it is to be followed blindly or accepted unquestioningly.
It invites humanity to use reasoning and to reflect on the teachings of The Qur'an to find the indisputable truth
and attain ultimate salvation.

@ The Muslims are treated as any other religious community by being told that, when it comes to justice and
judgment, they shall not be afforded any special concessions. For them, as for all human beings, reward shall be
commensurate with conduct and behavior in resonance with Divine Injunctions.

@ The battle between right and wrong, truth and falsehood, would never cease, but the final triumph shall
always be to the believers. Stand firm on the right; do not cross the limits set by Allah in matters of belief, acts of
worship, business dealings, morals and human relationships, etc., for it is the cause of all disorder and
corruption in material and religious life.

@ The Qur'an is Prophet Muhammad’s"” outstanding miracle that if all creation, human and jinn, were to work
together they could not produce the like of even one Qur'anic Sirah. However, the real miracles are those
which are inspired by teaching of The Qur'an and work within a human soul - the transformation which it is to
bring about in the world, the moving away of the great mountains of ignorance which are obstacles to the
spread of truth, and the awakening of those who are dead in spirit.

@ Allah does not change a people's condition unless they first change what is in themselves: thinking, attitude,
conduct and behavior—a mindset reflected in social behavior and public dealings.

e@ Allah orders social righteousness where materialism cannot dominate a Faithful's character and conduct;
urges fight against social corruption by preaching and drawing upon public opinion; forbids obscenity,
sodomy, adultery, fornication, commercial dishonesty and economic exploitation.

e It commands not to tamper with the property of orphans and under privileged; be fair and transparent in
business dealings, not to cheat and steal; speak for justice even if it affects one's family members; respect the
rights of the others: do not slander, do not malign; be generous but not a squanderer; be pure at heart and mind:
do not backbite, do not gossip, do not conspire, do not support vanity, do not bribe; be modest and
unpretentious: do not boast and do not show off.

@ Satan, the evil, has no real power over human beings. All it can do is to tempt and mislead those who allow
themselves to be misled. Thus they will have only to blame themselves for their choice of falling into error.

@ People need to be vigilant against all satanic temptations, realizing that as long as Allah's Laws are not
violated or abandoned, He will be forgiving and generous, otherwise His wrath can be overwhelming,
devastating.

e Affluence and economic injustice are first symptoms of corruption and oppression, and the two are
incompatible with a system based on divine revelation, and, for this very reason, the punishment for its
negligence is very severe.

@ Every person's ability to hear, to see and to think shall be interrogated and called to account at the Time of
Judgment.

@ Whoever looks forward with hope and awe to meeting one's Lord Supreme at the Time of Judgment, must do
deeds of righteousness, not associate anyone or anything in worship, reverence and obedience to Him, and
firmly believe in the Message of The Qur'an revealed onto His Last and Final Prophet to humanity, the Seal of
Prophets — Prophet Muhammad"’, may the blessings of Allah, His Angels and all righteous souls be on him to
eternity. Amin

Preface

First published in March 2013 under the banner ‘Anthologyof The Highlights of The Qur'an’ this
monumental work by my learned brother Badr Hashemi is now reappearing as ‘Journeying Through The
Qur'an’. It encapsulates direct translation of one-sixth of The Ayat/Statements of The Qur'an intended
for orderly conduct of life and living as peaceful and productive members of an inter-dependent global
family; remaining five-sixth repeatedly reiterates same universal values relatable to contextual realities
and situations at the relevant time. Direct translation of the Arabic Sacred Text is duly blended with the
context of respective revelations artfully flagged in italics. That medium was first employed by learned
brother for his six-volume land-mark scholarly project titled as ‘Paraphrasing of The Qur'an’ initiated in
late 1990's. Al-Hamd 0 Lillah, both sets of publications have been widely commended by a readership of
scholars of many faiths and not so learned too. It is specially useful for those who believe in peaceful co-
existence and actively build bridges without pre-conceived notions via inter-faith harmony.

Generally throughout human history, rational explanations were sought for the issues confronting
humanity in an attempt to comprehend ‘The Infinite’; the pursuit that shall always remain a mirage
regardless of one's belief and value system. The need for such a work becomes especially relevant in the
wake of emerging global scenario as issues of existence confront the humankind. Rising since 1970's, a
new type of religiosity, called 'fundamentalism',in many major religions including the three Divine with
‘political spirituality, increasingly intolerant in vision’ do not permit underplaying the urgency of inter-
faith understanding, as so painfully noted by Karen Armstrong.

The Qur'an authoritatively documents true origin of the Universe to declare humankind as best of His
creations bestowed complete mastery over its resources; provides most authentic historical account of
mankind with a comprehensive world view to encourage judicious use of natural endowments in an
inter-dependent Global Order at peace from within and without. Repeated expression of gratitude to the
Benevolent Creator, Rabb, Who so mercifully exposed all man-made hallow of the core fabrications in
the revealed religions made for petty mundane benefits, to urge guarding against subjective whims of the
misguided to exhort time and again virtues of the Path of Righteousness.

For the Faithful, core principles and specific provisions, whether voluntary or binding, were prescribed
for orderly regulation and conduct of life and living of an individual as a productive member of his
society, irrespective of cast, creed or race were expounded with utmost clarity. It spelt out the inescapable
regime of reward and punishment for every deed, big or small, with an unambiguous forewarning of
eventual accountability. In this divine scheme, consequences inherent in straying off the right course
pursued by His chosen and favorite slaves were expressly stated sans ambiguity. While reaffirming
human obligations, The Qur'an categorically and emphatically rules out coercion in matters of faith and
belief systems.

Uniquely concise in style, this work flags core principles and imperatives of the Divine Commandments,
primarily addressed to followers of Islamic Faith trained and tuned in contemporary learning in the West;
others are encouraged to read the Sacred Text with an open mind, to directly ascertain rational
explanations that may satisfy their inquisitive minds to facilitate informed choices without pre-
conceived prejudice or hostility to the extent possible. For the uninitiated among large readership of
educated classes in all faiths exposed to similar contemporary learning environment of the West, this
brief walk through is intended to cultivate, nurture and intensifyinter-faith harmony. Learned Brother's
own education at the global Centers of Excellence, living experience in many continents and intellectual
exposure to diverse cultural environs had motivated him to translate his deep understanding and
conviction that beyond the faith, all segments of readership are as inquisitive if not more, as the other.
This set of readers will also find this effort as an invaluably beneficial addition to the literature.

Islamabad Kh. Zaheer Ahmed
March 2016 Minister of State, Special Assistant to the Prime Minister
Formerly, Secretary to Government of Pakistan

title: The Qur’an by all accounts and standards, is the most stirring event of history. It has been the most
ocr_text:
Prelude

The Qur’an by all accounts and standards, is the most stirring event of history. It has been the most
intensely recited and extensively studied Book in all periods following its dissension upon the pure
heart and sincere soul of the last Prophet of Allah (peace be upon him). The Divine Book has been
the locus of reverence for the believers and focus of keen study by The scholars of Islam. This
tremendous scholarly enterprise evolved under the direct guidance of The Prophet (peace be upon
him), the prime teacher of The Qur’4n, its living embodiment and the ideal executer of its mission
in history. With the onward progress of Islamic educational tradition, the area of Qur’anic
scholarship exponentially grew and expanded in both vertical and horizontal dimensions.

Avery accomplished gentleman brother Badr Hashemi has included himself in the honorable list
of writers on The Qur’an. He has devoted his exceptional talents and energies to this labor of love
for several years and has delved in the depths of this shoreless ocean. He continues his utmost
intellectual concentration on understanding The Qur’4n with great zeal and fervor. In the present
work brother Badr Hashemi has made a commendable effort to relate the message of The Qur’an
to the pressing problems of modern man. He has made a successful attempt to capture what he saw
the core of The Qur’anic message so as to make available the fruits of his labor to the present day
reader. A great many people find it difficult to devote so much time to ponder over The Qur’anic
discourse as the author of ‘Journeying Through The Qur’an’. His work provides the reader with an
easy access to the essential teachings of the Divine Book sent down for the guidance of mankind.

The methodology evolved by the leaned author to bring home the answers of The Qur’an to the
problems of modern life is indeed a praiseworthy service to the formidable field of Qur’anic
studies. The details of this intelligently conceived methodology has been sufficiently explained by
the author himself. Further, he has provided simple English translation along with The Qur’anic
text and supplemented the literal rendering with brief explanatory words in italics. In this way, it
becomes easier for those readers who are less familiar with Qur’anic style, to comprehend the
Statements of The Qur’an throwing light on the relevant issues that have been dealt within the
selected verses.

The value of the author's effort lies in his earnest attempt to elaborate the contents of The Qur'anic
text wherever such an elaboration was required by the brevity of Qur'anic Statements. When The
Qur'an enters a theme of significance, its discourse is precedented or supplemented by similar
Statements at other places in different contexts.

Moreover, often times, The Qur'anic discourse proceeds on the basis of given premises. These
premises are intrinsic to The Qur'anic universe of knowledge and guidance. Without due notice of
this epistemological and teleological framework in which Qur'an speaks to man, it is not easy to
make sense of the perennial Qur'anic Message. The author of this work has supplied this necessary
clue to The Qur'anic world-view to the readers. This has been an essential task of every
commentator of The Qur'an. However, brother Badr Hashemi has performed this onerous task
without encumbering his work with copious foot notes.

In this way, the author has succeeded to bring forth a work of great utility in a single user-friendly
volume. He deserves our admiration and gratitude for this noble contribution. May Allah accept
his service to His Book and enable his readers to make the best use of this Valuable Companion to
the Study of The Qur’an.

Muhammad al-Ghazali, Ph. D.
Professor, Islamic Research Institute,
International Islamic University, Islamabad

Foreword

Brother Badr Hashemi's compilation of ‘Journeying Through The Qur'an’ contains much more than
selected portions of the Muslim Scripture. Additional materials provided beyond the title in
Introduction and explanatory statements, in italics, mostly from the primary (Qur'an) and secondary
(Traditions and Sayings of the Prophet Muhammad, Allah bless him always) sources are uniquely
invaluable in trustfully informing readers, which is generally absent or inconsistent in similar attempts
by earlier authors available elsewhere.

This novel approach adopted by Brother Badr Hashemi places his contributions in a class by itself,
especially if we keep the targeted audience for whom he undertook the challenge. This compilation
adds scholastic value and credibility because of the vast multilingual command, diversified cultural
exposure in formal professional settings, combined with religious training and expertise right from
author's childhood to the brief expose covered selectively but systematically, chapter-by-chapter, 1-
114, the compilation is a very worthy addition to meet hitherto unmet need of English-speaking people
interested in learning the gist of The Qur'anic Message written in literate English, as spoken in the US.

Within the same chapter, reading is enriched by sub-titles appropriately formulated to indicate the
intent and content of the Ayah/Statement under consideration. There is a common thread of emphasis
on behavioral, inter and intra communal, societal, and moral aspects of the guidance, without
sacrificing the mandatory aspects of acts of worship and the importance of obligatory religious duties
assigned for both the Creator and His creation, starting from parents, siblings, relatives to next-door
neighbors. Some of these aspects of The Qur'anic guidance have not been adequately covered in books
written by Orientalists or religious scholars, the former dwell on where the guidance lacks in their
perceived notion of gender equality, while the latter overemphasize the minute details of performing
religious duties.

Brother Badr Hashemi has devoted care and attention to what The Qur'an commands how to treat other
co-humans with whom believers come into contact during their mundane life on this earth, from
bedroom to boardroom. The compilation is emphasizing that guidance fromThe Qur'an is meant to lead
Mankind in all its affairs according to its basic ethics of Allah's Sovereignty, Prophetic Traditions,
Accountability in the Afterlife, without adopting any extremes of violating others rights to justice,

understanding the Message from The Qur'an itself and in convincing the reader of the argument,
augmentation provided appropriately by Brother Badr Hashemi.

The tone and approach of the body of compilation is non-sectarian, true to the spiritual intent of Allah-
consciousness, sincere toward leading to piety and righteousness, not adhering dogmatically to any
particular school-of-thought. The style of presenting the paraphrasing, notes in italics, and other textual
material is persuasive that is inviting both for Muslim and also for non-Muslim readers.
Comparatively, at several places, citations from Torah and Injil provided viz-a-viz Qur'an put an issue
in perspective from all three monotheistic faiths originating from the common patriarch Abraham,
peace be upon him.

This book has enabled advancing my personal learning of The Qur'anic message and modifying my
own knowledge-base of The Qur'anic understanding to serve Humanity at large. I trust it would
equally help in refining and fine tuning what everyone knows about The Qur'an, Islam, and Muslims.

title: Introduction
ocr_text:
Introduction

All Praise is for Allah - to whom be ascribed all perfection and majesty. He is the Eternal, the
Infinite and the Mighty, the Merciful and the Compassionate, the Creator and the Sustainer. I beg
for His mercy and forgiveness. I seek refuge in Allah from the Satanic, accursed and evil forces of
my soul and the surrounding social environment.

I testify that there is no one worthy of worshipful reverence and obedience except Allah: the
Singular, the Unity. I testify that Muhammad bin Abd Allah bin Abd Al-Mittalib Al-Hashemi is
His obedient servant, His Prophet and His Emissary. He designated him to be 'The Seal of the
Prophets’ and 'Mercy for Humanity.’

Prophet Muhammad was and shall always be the most remarkable man to have received and
preached the Divine Word, led the greatest spiritual revolution, transformed a man-centered
society to Allah-centered nation, initiated fundamental social and political reforms, established a
dynamic and powerful socio-economic order that changed the worlds of human thought and
action, and left a most profound influence on history, culture and civilization. May the eternal
peace and blessings of Allah, the angels and the righteous souls be upon him. Amin.

The Qur'an is the recited speech of Allah, the Exalted. The Qur'anic imperative 'Qul', i.e., read,
recite, state, declare, announce or proclaim - which introduces more than three hundred passages -
is areminder that the texts are to be read, recited, understood, practiced and preached.

The Prophet, Allah bless him always with honor, is reported by al-Bokhari to have said: 'Read the
Qur'an for you will be rewarded at the rate of ten good deeds for reading every letter of The Qur'an.
Note that I do not say that alif-lam-mim is one letter; rather, alif is one letter, lam is another, and
mim is yet another.’

He would often recite the Qur'an in a low but audible voice, and at times ask others to recite for
im. He would advise his followers to 'recite/read even one Ayah/Statement with mind fully
attuned to its meaning as it would be better than offering one hundred raka' of nawafil’ - the
optional Prayers. He further said: 'You can return to Allah nothing better than which came from
Him; recite/read The Qur'an!' In fact, a community that is given the Scripture and continues to
recite/read it and live by it, is ina relationship through which Allah continues to guide it.

The tradition of reciting/reading The Qur'an appears to be slowly diminishing both in the Arabic
speaking countries as well as in the others. On the basis of a snapshot survey informally conducted
during my visits to and/or stays in Algeria, Iran, Iraq, Indonesia, Jordan, Morocco, Malaysia,
Pakistan, Turkey, Syria and interactions with Muslim communities in Canada, Japan, Taiwan,
South Africa, UK and USA during 1992-2001 and later in 2005-07, notwithstanding statistically
insignificant size of the sample, it transpired that only about three percent of the educated Muslims
ad read The Qur'an once in their lifetime, while about seven percent were content with selective
reading of the Scripture, with a statistically insignificant number able to develop a rudimentary
understanding or any meaningful comprehension of the Divine Message.

The trend was more disheartening among the college/university-going youth, especially those
who were being raised in the English speaking environment in their native places and/or overseas,
where they were confronted with challenges of identity in the perspective of growing influence of
Western culture and hate campaign against Islam and Muslims.

It may not be unreasonable to argue that the situation may have worsened in the intervening period
due to increasing number of population entering that age-group combined by reduced family time
for in-house teaching and training as well as an increasingly hostile attitude against Islam.
Notwithstanding the challenges, it appeared that their lack of inclination was, inter alia, due to
huge volume of The Qur'anic body and non availability of comprehensible and friendly English
translations.

title: Introduction
ocr_text:
Introduction

The concept of the existence of a Supreme Divine Entity is a living reality
with humankind — from eternity to infinity. The Qur’an (Q.14:04) tells
us that Allah — The One Lord Supreme has been sending Messengers to
various nations with Messages in their own language. In each language,
the Names or the Attributes represented by different sounds and symbols
were used for The One Lord Supreme.

The One Lord Supreme was known as ‘El Shaddai’ to Abraham, Isaac,
and Jacob (Exodus 06:03). Later, He spoke to Moses as ‘Yahweh’ and
‘Elohim’ (Exodus 06:12); ‘Elah’, an Aramaic expression, written in the
Tanakh (Jeremiah 10:11) describes the Jews’ God. Jesus addressed Him
as ‘Eloi’ (Mark 15:34); and, to Muhammad ‘Allah’ was the proper name
for The One Lord Supreme (Q.112:01). Interestingly, the Divine Names
of Elohim, Elah, Eloi and Elah (Q.43:84)/Allah are etymologically related
and carry a close common thematic and audio denominator.

The Towrat — Old Testament — a fifteenth century BC document, lists at
least 33 Divine Attributes: None beside Him, None before Him, None
like to Him, None Good but He, Fills Heaven and Earth, God Is light,
Love, Unsearchable, Eternal, Omnipotent, Omniscient, Omnipresent,
Immutable, Glorious, Most High, Perfect, Peace, Holy, Just, True,
Upright, Righteous, Good, Great, Gracious, Merciful, Compassionate,
Forgiving, Sanctifier, Unique, Transcendent, Savior, Owner, Master to be
Worshipped in Spirit and in Truth.

The Injil - New Testament - preceding Islam by about six centuries,
states the Divine Attributes: Salvation is through His Name, Believers
are to gather in His Name, Prayer is to be made in His Name. It stresses
His Strength, Sovereignty, and Supremacy. The Everlasting Divine
Entity emphasizes His Unchangeableness and is connected with His
Inexhaustibleness.

title: The Qur’an — Final Testament - uses a large number of Names/Attributes
ocr_text:
The Qur’an — Final Testament - uses a large number of Names/Attributes
for Allah which indicates continuity of the Divine Names/Attributes from
the Towrat and the Injil. It makes an explicit reference to these Names/
Attributes as ‘Al-Asma al-Husna’ — The Names, The Uniquely Beautiful
- on four occasions:

*  Q.07:180 —To Allah belongs The Names, The Uniquely
Beautiful; so call Him by them.

* Q.17:110 - Call upon Him either by The Name of Allah,
or by The Name of Al-Rahman; by whichever Name you
call upon Him, for His are The Names, The Uniquely

Beautiful;

* Q.20:08 - To Him alone belongs The Names, The
Uniquely Beautiful.

* Q.59:24 — For Him are The Names, The Uniquely
Beautiful.

The Names/Attributes portray expositions about the Divine Essence
rather than doctrinal expositions concerning the nature of Allah — the
One God. The Prophet Muhammad, Allah bless him always, is reported
to have stated: ‘Allah created man in His Own Image.’ Mohyuddin Ibn
Al-‘Arabr (b.1165) takes it further that *....upon the Form of Allah, so
he (man) was also created upon the Form of Other Names — that is why
Q.02:30 mentions that Allah taught Adam “All The Names.’ Hence, man
displays an indefinite variety of divine aspects.’

The Hadith literature adds the expression of ‘Al-Sifat al-‘Ulya’ - The
Exalted Attributes - to the Qur’anic title of ’Al-Asma al-Husna.’ While
the Qur’an does not explicitly use the phrase ‘99 Names of Allah’, it is
the Prophet, Allah bless him always, who is reported to have said: “There
are 99 Names of Allah; one hundred minus one. Whoever enumerates
them (or commits to memory) would get into Paradise.’ Reported by Al-
Bokhari in [70]6410.

Four of the 99 Blessed Names have a special significance in the sense
that 4 of the 114 Surahs of The Qur’adn are named after them: Al-Nir
(24), Fatir (35), Ghafir (40) and Al-Rahman (55). The Muslim Opening
Prayer of every Salat is embedded with a Two-Word Phrase addressed to

title: Allah: ‘Wa Tabara-ka-smuka,’ i.e. And Full of Blessings is Your Name.
ocr_text:
Allah: ‘Wa Tabara-ka-smuka,’ i.e. And Full of Blessings is Your Name.
Q.67:01, etc. state ‘Tabaraka Alladhi,’ i.e. Blessed is He. Again Q.23:14
asserts ‘Fa-Tabarak Allah’ — Blessed is Allah. Thus, whatever Name He
may have given to Himself has its own blessings uniquely - both spiritual
and material, bounty, luminosity and healing power to the one who recites
it with faith, repeatedly and regularly over time.

The Attributes - as adjectives, word constructs, or derivatives from Arabic
infinitive verbal noun are thematic in content and manifestation and their
occurrence in the Qur’an varies from one time to as many as more than
one hundred times. However, not every verb can be considered a Divine
Name/Attribute. In form, however, every Name/Attribute is a masculine
singular.

They appear in 86 of 114 Strahs. The initial Sirahs contain a major
occurrence of almost all of them. They occur solo as Al-Samad, Al-
Wahhab, Al-Ghaniyye, etc; while those in pairs — 59 — add a different
dimension to the mosaic, like Al-Rahman Al-Rahim (pronounced as
Ar-Rahmaan-ira-Raheem), Al-Tawwab Al-Rahim (pronounced as At-
Tawwaab-ur-Raheem) and Al-Hayy Al-Qayyiim (pronounced as Al-
Hayy-ul-Qayyuum), etc., three, four, five and more appear together with
much lesser frequency. Q.59:22-24 contains 17 of them in one place.

Some of ‘The 99 Names’ do not occur literally in the Qur’an like, for
instance, Al-Qabidz, Al-Basit, Al-Rafi’y, Al-Mo’izz and Al-Mu’akhkhir,
etc. Hence the list is liable to contain some variants. Each of ‘The 99
Names and Attributes listed in this book is in the order that it is enumerated
in the related Hadith. With every Name/Attribute the expression of ‘Jalla
Jalaluh’ is added to signify Allah’s Majesty and Exaltation, where in case
of ‘Jallah’, first letter ‘I’ is assimilated with second letter ‘I’ to indicate the
doubling of its sound in pronunciation with stress on its accent - Shadd.

The Prophet, Allah bless him always, advised his companions to keep
their hearts illuminated with the Dhikr, i.e. Devotional Remembrance of
Allah. And one way to do so is by repeatedly reciting ‘The 99 Names’
while sitting in seclusion, as it is in this Remembrance that the believers’
hearts would find inner peace, solace and satisfaction — Q.13:28. Thus
the Dhikr of ‘The 99 Names’ is one of the most diligent devotions as it
illuminates one’s heart, thereby leading to fulfill the requisites of Faith,

ocr_text:
which entitles The Faithful to hope for Allah’s Mercy and Compassion in
this life, and Success in the Life After This Life.

The Qur’an directs The Faithful to invoke and solicit the Blessings of
Allah by His Names — Q.07:180. Thus, as a part of the social etiquette and
mannerism the Muslims recite ‘Bi-Ism-Allah,’ pronounced as ‘Bismillah,’
meaning ‘With the Name of Allah, before starting any act of worship,
work, ceremony, social gathering, or taking meals/drinks, etc.

Interestingly, each of the 28 letters of Arabic alphabet carries a numerical
value; e.g. its first letter ‘Alif’ has 01, second letter “Ba’ has 02, and
so forth. Based on this premise, ‘786’ is the most popular numerical
equivalent for ‘Bismillah’ among The Faithful. Thus, carrying the thread
forward, each of the Divine Name/Attribute also has its own numerical
equivalent, which is stated at the bottom of each epithet for the benefit of
those who may wish to benefit.

‘The Divine 99’ are normally recited in a state of physical and spiritual
purity as part of the Dhikr and making a plea to Allah. Hence, the
expression ‘Ya’ appears as prefix to the Name; e.g. Ya Allah, Ya Rahman,
etc. where ‘Ya’ means O’ - as an address to the addressee. For purposes of
pronunciation, see Transliteration, Transcription and Sound Equivalents
at Page 260.

This book comprises three sections. Section | presents all the Single 99
Attributes as they appear in the Qur’an and Hadith literature. Section 2
presents those of The Attributes that appear in pairs — The Composite
Attributes. These are neither plurals nor morakkab. In both sections
the Names/Attributes are presented in Arabic with transliteration and
pronunciation; references either to Sirah:Ayah/Statement or source
of Hadith appear below each. Meanings and Blessings of the Names/
Attributes, both spiritual and material, are also briefly stated which have
been adapted from some of the literature mentioned in Bibliography. The
blessings may shower on those who believe that Allah's Holy Names and
Majestic Attributes are the fountainhead of barakat. Section 3 presents a
Glimpse of Images of Divine Fragrance as it glows up in various Ayat.

Great care has been exercised in transliterating the Arabic Names/
Attributes as also relating the Sirah numbers with those of Ayat/

meaning ‘originates’) in Q.29:19; 85:13; etc. Al-Mubdi is listed as a

Approximate Meaning: The One from whom everything originates.
The One who causes the beginning of everything. He who creates
existence out of nothing. The meaning of Allah’s qualities of Al-
Mubdi — The Beginner and Al-Mu’id - The Restorer is to bring
another into being. When this bringing into being has no precedent
in terms of an act similar to it, it is called a beginning. If there is a
precedent in terms of an act similar to it, it is called a restoration
- Mu’id. Allah began the creation of human and jinn, and it is He
would also restore them. All things first originated from Him, and,
then are restored to Him.

Blessings, if Allah Wills: Repeating it a few times every day on the
expectant mother - who may be afraid of losing the baby via still-
birth or abortion, shall cause her to be relieved of the apprehension,
and blessed with a baby.

title: Statements. Nevertheless, it is quite probable that some inaccuracies may
ocr_text:
Statements. Nevertheless, it is quite probable that some inaccuracies may
have crept in as part of human weakness, or I may have overlooked a
point out of ignorance. I should appreciate if such errors and omissions
are advised via hashemibadr@gmail.com

The Divine 99 Names are in Arabic. These have been presented in this
book as in their written form; not as in their spoken form. The two forms
have a subtle difference which has been taken care of by adding a sub-title
“Pronunciation.”

The spirit, the beauty, the eloquence, the depth and the comprehensiveness
of these Arabic Divine 99 Names can never be captured by any other
language. Translations can be dull and convey the apparent meaning but
remain devoid of the true spirit and divine sanctity. Strongly mindful
of these limitations and my inadequacies, I have suggested a range of
Approximate Meanings, and supplemented translations with extended
wording by way of paraphrasing, wherever necessary.

This work is not entirely mine. My wife Shahida and sister Apa Bushra,
both educationists, provided extensive research support for over a year.
The devotional artwork was created by Nayyer, talented wife of my friend,
Prof. Ehsan Rashid, former Vice Chancellor of Karachi University. I am
deeply indebted to Shahida, Apa Bushra and Mme Nayyer.

I owe special thanks to the Islamic Research Institute, International
Islamic University, Islamabad, for consenting me to use the Arabic
Calligraphy from one its publications, titled: To God Belong The Names
Most Beautiful.

My audience is an educated reader, not a scholar with partisan inclination.
Thus, the text has been purposely kept simple without using jargon of
theology and going in to the depth and expense of explaining the varying
patterns of the Divine Attributes in the perspective of the circumstances
during the time of their respective revelations.

I seek Allah Jalla Jalaluhu’s guidance to accomplish a faithful translation,
transliteration, transcription and transmission of His Majestic Names
and Exalted Attributes embedded with true devotional spirit. May Jalla
Jalaluhu grant acceptance to this humble endeavor dedicated with awe
and humility to His Name: The Greatest Name, Al-Ism Al-‘Azam. Amin.

grows and develops, and then dies and disappears till the Time of
The Resurrection, when all human and jinn will be brought back to
life into a new dimension of existance.

The Single Attributes

This Section comprises the Names/Attributes that occur as Single
or in combination with other(s) in The Qur’an. The ones occurring
in pairs have been split and counted as Singles on the premise that
it is the Singles that have been conventionally enumerated as “The
99.” The serialization of these from 01 to 14 in this Section follows
the sequence as it appears in Q.59:22-24. The remaining have been
cherry-picked as they appear in most of the 114 Sirah. In total there
are 72 Names/Attributes that are directly mentioned; these are marked
in green, e.g. Al-Rahman.

Thus to complete the conventional number of 99, 27 comprise such
epithets which are either word constructs, or derivatives from Arabic
infinitive verbal noun/nomen verbi mentioned in The Qur’an, and/or
the Hadith literature. These 27 are marked in blue e.g. Al-Muhsi. It
may, however, be mentioned that the specific Hadith which contains
the list of 99 epithets was recorded by Al-Tirmidhi, Ibn Majah and Abi
Dawid. This Hadith is considered weak by Al-Tirmidhi himself and
others including Al-Bayhaqi, Ibn Hazim, Ibn Taymiya, Ibn Kathir, Ibn
Hajr, Ibn Baz and Al-Albant, etc. Nevertheless, given that the Prophet,
Allah bless him always, did say that there are 99 Divine Names, the
classical and contemporary scholars take a lenient stance on the report
by Al-Tirmidhi.

The Divine Attribute of ‘Al-Wadiid’— Q.85:14 and Q. 11:90 — meaning
‘loving’ is articulately balanced by its counterpoint in Q.05:54,
depicting Divine Love answered by human love: ‘He loves them as
they love Him.

The Attributes of ‘Al-Barr — The Maker (Q.02:54; 59:24), ‘Al-Badi’y’
— The Originator (Q.02:117; 06:101), ‘Al-Musawwir’ — The Shaper

Gl-Nur Jalla Jalaluh

Related Sirah: Ayah—occurs only once as Allah-u Nir-us-Samawat-i

Approximate Meaning: The Light. The Radiant. The Light is Allah’s
quality of being the visible by means of which everything is made
visible. When existence is contrasted with non-existence, it becomes
obvious that visibility pertains to existence, and that there is no
darkness darker than non-existence. Existence is a light which flows
freely upon all things from The Light of Allah’s Essence. Therefore,
Allah is The Light of the heavens and the earth — Q.24:35. Just as
there is not a particle of the light of the sun which does not point to
the existence of the illuminating sun, so is there not a particle of the
existence which does not, by the mere possibility of its existence,
point to the necessary existence of its Creator.

Blessings, if Allah Wills: Those who read/recite “Ya Allah Ya Nir’
1,001 times every morning, days in and days out, shall be blessed
with spiritual enlightenment. Mystics normally repeat this Name 256
times every Friday. Its recitation also helps in healing eye related

title: The Attribute of ‘Rabb’ is particularly significant as it conveys
ocr_text:
The Attribute of ‘Rabb’ is particularly significant as it conveys
the basic functional Divine Concept which not only comprise the
fostering, upbringing and nourishing His Creation but also regulating,
completing, accomplishing, sustaining and perfection of the existence
of His Creation. It also means Originator of things and their Combiner
to create new forms. The lexicons of Arabic language speak of all
of them, and more, when they give the detailed meaning of the root
‘Rabb.’

It is open to discussion whether some or all of these epithets may
be considered either to supplement or to replace ‘The 27’ that do not
directly appear in The Qur’an. The additional ‘identified’ Attributes
have been listed with reference to specific Sirah:Ayah/Ayat in the
later part of this Section, titled ‘The 99 Plus.’ While referencing to
Stirah:Ayah, the first number denotes the Sarah, the second number
denotes the Ayah; thus, 02:20 would mean Second Sirah and Twenth
Ayah.

The adjectives — Al-Asma Al-Sifat - used for portraying the Divine
Attributes are not exclusive. There are several instances in The Qur’an
where these have also been used for non-divine entities and purposes.

| Section 2 |

The Composite Attributes

Almost all of the Divine Attributes marked in green in Section -1 appear
in an equal number of Pairs like Al-Rahman Al-Rahim, phrased here as
Composite Attributes, but are not Asma al-Morakkab. These Attributes
carry a pre-fix ‘al’ to make a common noun to a proper noun; as also does
“‘tanwin’ on a common noun to make it a proper noun.

Tanwin is also referred to as Nunation where the signs of short vowels
are doubled, and are pronounced with the addition of the sound of ‘an’ (as
in gun), ‘in’ (as in fin), or ‘un’ (as in sun) which takes place only at the
end of a vowel, and is shown as a syllable in writing as part of the word.
Q.03:34 states the Attribute of Sami-un ‘Alim-un, where ‘un’ is tanwin/
nunation; and Q.03:35 closes with Al-Sam7’ Al-‘Alim, with ‘al’ pre-fix,
both conveying the same meaning.

This Section considers all the 59 Composite Attributes both with a pre-fix
of ‘al’ as well as with tanwin/nunation. 16 of these are common to both.
It restricts translation and paraphrasing of The Composite Attributes to
one Ayah.

It would be unusual for The Composite Attribute to appear in the
beginning or middle of the Ayah as Q.20:114; their appearance is usual
at the closing of the Ayah/Ayat. The Pairs repeat themselves in various
permutations and combinations. These occurrences are linked with each
other like honey-comb [Illustration on Pages 220-222]. Within the Pairs,
Al-‘Aziz Al-Hakim ranks highest, followed by Al-‘Aziz Al-Rahim and
Al-Sam?’ Al-‘Alim, and so forth.

The repeated variations of The Composite and Single Attributes
throughout The Qur’an and The Composites in this Section are meant to
stress the moral odiousness and intellectual futility of attributing Divine
Qualities to any entity, real or myth, human or jinn, spirit or saint, other
than Allah — The One God - Q.07:180.

Allah Jalla Jalaluh

Pronunciation: Allah; Allaah with stress in accent on letter /I/ to
signify the doubling of its sound in pronunciation.

Occurrence: 2,697 times in The Qur’an. Q.20:14 stresses: “Surely,
I am Allah. There is no entity worthy of worship and reverence
except Me. Worship Me alone. And keep up your prayers for My
Remembrence.’ Allah and Elah are two different expressions. The
former is not a contraction of the later Al-Elah. Elah occurring 147
times in the Qur’an has been used sometimes meaning Allah, the
One God, like Allah-o Elahuw-Wahid in Q.04:171; 22:34; Elahu-
kum Elahuw-Wahid in Q.02:163; and Huwalla-dhi Fis-Sama-i Elah
wa fil-Ardz-i Elah in Q.43:84, etc. However, most of the times it
occurs in negation of more than One God, Allah, e.g. La Elaha; La
Elaha [la-Allah; La Tattakhidhi Elahain. While Allah is Singular
and has no plural; Aliha is the plural of Elah.

Approximate Meaning: The Greatest Proper Name for the Almighty.
The One God, Singular, who does not have a gender, parents,
siblings, spouse, daughters and/or sons. Allah is above and beyond
all description; “There is nothing whatsoever like Him’- Q.42:11 and
112:04. Faith in Allah is the fulcrum of Islamic Monotheism and
obedience to His Will is the focus of the Muslim way of life. This
belief is called “Tawhid’ and it constitutes the foremost article of the
Islamic Profession of Faith. To attribute divinity to a created entity
is the only unpardonable sin mentioned in The Qur’an — 04:48, 116.

Blessings, if Allah Wills: Reciting “Ya Allah’ 1,000 times daily will
makes one’s heart free from all sorts of doubts, apprehensions and
suspicions, and instill determination and faith. One suffering from
incurable diseases should repeat this Name many a time, every day,
then pray to Allah for healing, health and recovery.

Numerical Equivalent: 36.

ocr_text:
Ql-Rahman Falla Fatatuh

Pronunciation: Al-Rahman. Ar-Rahmaan with stress in accent on letter
/t/ to signify the doubling of its sound in pronunciation; /h/ a harsher
sound than the English initial /h/ may occur medially and in word-final
position as well; it is produced by expelling the air through a narrowed
throat in much the same way as one tries to clear one’s throat. /A/ is
pronounced as in /longer a/ as in cab (not as in cake).

Related Sirah: Ayat— Occurs 57 times either as Al-Rahman or Rahman-
un (Active Particle Noun) in Q.01:02;13:30;17:110;19:26,44,45,58,61,
69,75,78,85,88,91,92,96;20:05,90, 108,109; 21:26,36,42; 25:26; 36:52;
43:33: 50:33; 55:01; 67:19,29; 78:38; and in combination with other
Divine Attributes as Al-Rahman Al-Rahim in Q.01:02, 02:163, 27:30,
41:02; 59:22; as Rabbuk-um Al-Rahman in Q.20:90; and as Rabb-un
Al-Rahman-o Al-Musta’an in Q.21:112.

Q.17:110 reads as ‘... Invoke Allah or invoke Al-Rahman....’implies
that Al-Rahman is also His Proper Name in addition to Allah, Jalla
Jalaluh.

Also occurs as Arham-ur-Rahimin (where Arham means ‘most
compassionate’) in Q.12:64, 92; 59:22; 41:02; and Khyr-ur-Rahimin
(where Khyr means ‘better’) in Q.23:109,118; and Dhiir-Rahma (where
Dhi is Demonstrative Pronoun) in Q.06:133; 18:58.

Approximate Meaning: The Lord of Infinite Mercy. The Dispenser of
Grace. The Benevolent. The Beneficent. The Merciful to All. The Most
Gracious.

Blessings, if Allah Wills: This Name is recited repeatedly to get rid of
calamities and misfortunes. If recited 500 times after every Mandatory
Prayer during the night-day cycle, one would be forgiven one’s sinful
offences; and, it would improve one’s memory and make it intelligently
alert. In case it is recited 100 times after the Early Morning Prayers,
al-Fajr, it rids one of hard-heartedness towards others and softens the
attitudes of others towards the one who recites.

| Epilogue

It was noted in the ‘Introduction’ that a report carried by both al-
Bokhari and Muslim, on the authority of Abii Hurayrah, suggests that
The Prophet, Allah bless him always, said: ‘There are 99 Names of
Allah, one hundred minus one, whoever enumerates them would enter
the Paradise.’ But The Prophet is neither reported to have specified nor
elaborated The 99 Exalted Names.

It was observed in ‘Section 1’ that listing of the 99 Exalted Names/
Attributes, one by one, was a report carried by Tirmidi, Ibn Majah
and Abii Dawid, but not by Bokhari and Muslim; and that this Hadith
was considered weak even by Tirmidi himself, who was joined in his
opinion by luminaries like al-Bayhaqi, Ibn Hazim, Ibn Taymiya, Ibn
Kathir, Ibn Hajr, Ibn Baz and al-Bani, etc.

Thus it was concluded that while ‘The 99’ number is considered
authentic by all and sundry, listing of specific Exalted Names/
Attributes, in varying versions, does not meet the standard of scrutiny,
notwithstanding the fact that some of The Exalted Names/Attributes
in every version do not match one another.

Moreover, actions associated with Allah, Exalted and Almighty, are
numerous as illustrated in ‘Section 3’. For example, He removes
evil, He hurls the truth, He will distinguish them, He is a Witness
of Retribution, Receiver of Repentance, Forgiver of Sins, Merger of
Night into Day, Merger of Day into Night, Bringer of Life from death,
and Bringer of Death from Life, The Everlasting Essence, The Willer,
The Thing, etc.

So if deriving ‘Names from Actions’ be permitted, then one may
derive His Exalted Names/Attributes as: The Remover, The Hurler of
Truth, The Distinguisher, The Cultivator, The Sower, The Thrower,
The Humbling One, and The One Who Decrees; and such ‘Derived
Names’ would be countless.

in Your Knowledge of hidden things,’ and, thus has not informed us of
these, shows that the Exalted Names/Attributes are not limited to any
specific number or any known version.

Let’s revert to the Hadith, authenticated by all and sundry, that “There
are 99 Names of Allah, one hundred minus one, whoever enumerates
them would enter the Paradise,’ and taking the point further, if the
Exalted Names/Attributes were to exceed ‘99’ and one was to estimate,
for example, that there were a thousand of such epithets, yet whoever

title: enumerated ‘99’ of them, would be entitled to the Paradise. The

enumerated ‘99’ of them, would be entitled to the Paradise. The
question may be raised as to why ‘99’ has been singled out although
all are the Names of Allah, Exalted and Almighty.

Exploring it further may suggest that it is quite possible that some of
the Exalted Names may differ in excellence because their meanings
differ in eminence and distinction, so that ‘99’ of them will bring
together a variety of meanings which tell of The Divine Majesty, which
another set of meanings, would not be able to bring together, and so
that one particular combination is possessed of greater eminence and
distinction than the other.

It has been mentioned earlier in the book that Allah, Exalted and
Almighty, has The Supreme Name — ‘Al-Ism Al-A’zam’ — which is
neither explicitly mentioned in The Qur’an nor in the Hadith, although
a lot of conjunctures have floated around since the seventh century
AD. Nevertheless, it would be pertinent to examine whether ‘Al-Ism
Al-A’zam’ is included in the known Exalted Names/Attributes; if it is,
which one would it be; and if it is not, then, how can it be distinguished
by greater dignity and yet be outside the Exalted Names?

It would not be unfair to argue that ‘Al-Ism Al-A’zam’ may not have
been included in the listing carried by Tirmidi, Ibn Majah and Abii
Dawid, yet it is also probable that it may be ‘hidden’ in one of the ones
mentioned in The Qur’an, and listed under ‘The 99 Plus’, ‘Section 2’
and/or ‘Section 3’. The Prophet, Allah bless him always, is reported in
Tirmidi (5.517) to have said: The Supreme Name is in these two Ayat:

Q.02.Al-Baqgarah:163
And you Allah is the One Allah: there is no entity worthy of

worship except Him, The Infinitely Merciful to all,
The Ever-Compassionate to everyone.

Alif. Lam. Mim. Allah — there is no entity worthy of worship except
Him, the Ever-Living, the Self-Subsistent.

It is reported by Ibn Majah that The Prophet, Allah bless him always,
heard a man praying and making a plea: ‘By Allah, I ask You that I
may testify that You are Allah, and there is no entity worthy of worship
except You, the Eternal One, Who is neither giving birth to anyone,
nor being born of anyone, and there is no one equal or comparable to
Him.’

So The Prophet said: ‘By the One in Whose Hand is my soul, he has
invoked Allah, The Most High, by His Supreme Name — the Name by
which He answers when He is called upon with it, and gives when He
is petitioned with it.’

The Prophet’s quotation regarding ‘99’ and specifying it as ‘one
hundred minus one’ explains his point of view that ‘Allah, Who is
odd (One), loves what is odd.’ This pertains to His Essence and His
Divinity, and there is no restriction on their number and its principle.
He does not make them ‘100’ just because He loves what is odd; hence
99"

It is Allah, Exalted and Almighty, Who knows best what is right in
such and all matters. It is also He, Who is The Source to which we ever
return, time and again, for truth and guidance.
